section.heading: 1.2. Mathematical Models: A Catalog of Essential Functions
section.paragraph: A mathematical model is a mathematical description (often by means of a function or an equation) of a real-world phenomenon such as the size of a population, the demand for a product, the speed of a falling object, the concentration of a product in a chemical reaction, the life expectancy of a person at birth, or the cost of emissions reductions. The purpose of the model is to understand the phenomenon and perhaps to make predictions about future behavior.

Given a real-world problem, our first task in the mathematical modeling process is to formulate a mathematical model by identifying and naming the independent and dependent variables and making assumptions that simplify the phenomenon enough to make it mathematically tractable. We use our knowledge of the physical situation and our mathematical skills to obtain equations that relate the variables. In situations where there is no physical law to guide us, we may need to collect data (either from the Internet or a library or by conducting our own experiments) and examine the data in the form of a table in order to discern patterns. From this numerical representation of a function we may wish to obtain a graphical representation by plotting the data. The graph might even suggest a suitable algebraic formula in some cases.

The second stage is to apply the mathematics that we know (such as the calculus that will be developed throughout this book) to the mathematical model that we have formulated in order to derive mathematical conclusions. Then, in the third stage, we take those mathematical conclusions and interpret them as information about the original real-world phenomenon by way of offering explanations or making predictions. The final step is to test our predictions by checking against new real data. If the predictions don’t compare well with reality, we need to refine our model or formulate a new model and start the cycle again. Figure 1 illustrates the process of mathematical modeling.

section.paragraph: A mathematical model is never a completely accurate representation of a physical situation—it is an idealization. A good model simplifies reality enough to permit mathematical calculations but is accurate enough to provide valuable conclusions. It is important to realize the limitations of a model.

There are many different types of functions that can be used to model relationships observed in the real world. In what follows, we discuss the behavior and graphs of some of these functions and give examples of situations appropriately modeled by such functions.
section.heading: Linear Models
section.paragraph: When we say that $$y$$ is a linear function of $$x$$ , we mean that the graph of the function is a line, so we can use the slope-intercept form of the equation of a line to write a formula for the function as
$$y = f(x) = mx + b$$
where $$m$$ is the slope of the line and $$b$$ is the $$y$$ -intercept.
The coordinate geometry of lines is reviewed in Appendix B.

A characteristic feature of linear functions is that they change at a constant rate. For instance, Figure 2 shows a graph of the linear function $$f(x) = 3x - 2$$ and a table of sample values. Notice that whenever $$x$$ increases by $$0.1$$ , the value of $$f(x)$$ increases by $$0.3$$ . So $$f(x)$$ increases three times as fast as $$x$$ . This means that the slope of the graph of $$y = 3x - 2$$ , namely $$3$$ , can be interpreted as the rate of change of $$y$$ with respect to $$x$$ .

example.heading: Example 1

list.item: (a) As dry air moves upward, it expands and cools. If the ground temperature is $$20{}_{}^{}$$ and the temperature at a height of $$1$$ km is $$10{}_{}^{}$$ , express the temperature $$T$$ (in $${}_{}^{}{}$$ ) as a function of the height $$h$$ (in kilometers), assuming that a linear model is appropriate.
(b) Draw the graph of the function in part (a). What does the slope represent?
(c) What is the temperature at a height of $$2.5$$ km?

example.paragraph: Solution

list.item: (a) Because we are assuming that $$T$$ is a linear function of $$h$$ , we can write $$T = mh + b$$ We are given that $$T = 20$$ when $$h = 0$$ , so $$20 = m \cdot 0 + b = b$$ In other words, the $$y$$ -intercept is $$b = 20$$ . We are also given that $$T = 10$$ when $$h = 1$$ , so $$10 = m \cdot 1 + 20$$ The slope of the line is therefore $$m = 10 - 20 = - 10$$ and the required linear function is $$T = - 10h + 20$$

(b) The graph is sketched in Figure 3. The slope is $$m = - 10{}_{}^{} \slash {km}$$ and this represents the rate of change of temperature with respect to height. Figure 3 Details A line with negative slope is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The horizontal axis labeled h is displayed from 0 to 5 in increments of 1 unit. The vertical axis labeled T is displayed from negative 10 to 25 in increments of 5 units. The line labeled T = negative 10 h + 20 begins at the point (0, 20), goes down and to the right, crosses the x axis at (2, 0), and extends downward in the fourth quadrant.
(c) At a height of $$h = 2.5$$ km, the temperature is $$T = - 10(2.5) + 20 = - 5{}_{}^{}$$

section.paragraph: If there is no physical law or principle to help us formulate a model, we construct an empirical model, which is based entirely on collected data. We seek a curve that “fits” the data in the sense that it captures the basic trend of the data points.

section.heading: Polynomials
section.paragraph: A function $$P$$ is called a polynomial if

where $$n$$ is a nonnegative integer and the numbers $$a_{0},a_{1},a_{2},\ldots,a_{n}$$ are constants called the coefficients of the polynomial. The domain of any polynomial is $${\mathbb{R}} = \left( {- \infty,\infty} \right)$$ . If the leading coefficient $$a_{n} \neq 0$$ , then the degree of the polynomial is $$n$$ . For example, the function
is a polynomial of degree $$6$$ .

A polynomial of degree $$1$$ is of the form $$P(x) = mx + b$$ and so it is a linear function. A polynomial of degree $$2$$ is of the form $$P(x) = ax^{2} + bx + c$$ and is called a quadratic function. Its graph is always a parabola obtained by shifting the parabola $$y = ax^{2}$$ , as we will see in Section 1.3. The parabola opens upward if $$a > 0$$ and downward if $$a < 0$$ (see Figure 7).

section.paragraph: The general shape of the graph of $$f(x) = x^{n}$$ depends on whether $$n$$ is even or odd. If $$n$$ is even, then $$f(x) = x^{n}$$ is an even function and its graph is similar to the parabola $$y = x^{2}$$ . If $$n$$ is odd, then $$f(x) = x^{n}$$ is an odd function and its graph is similar to that of $$y = x^{3}$$ . Notice from Figure 12, however, that as $$n$$ increases, the graph of $$y = x^{n}$$ becomes flatter near $$0$$ and steeper when $$|x| \geqslant 1$$ . (If $$x$$ is small, then $$x^{2}$$ is smaller, $$x^{3}$$ is even smaller, $$x^{4}$$ is smaller still, and so on.)

(ii) $$\mathbf{a} = 1 \slash \mathbf{n}$$ , where $$\mathbf{n}$$ is a positive integer

The function $$f(x) = x^{1 \slash n} = \sqrt[n]{x}$$ is a root function. For $$n = 2$$ it is the square root function $$f(x) = \sqrt{x}$$ , whose domain is $$\lbrack 0,\infty)$$ and whose graph is the upper half of the parabola $$x = y^{2}$$ . [See Figure 13(a).] For other even values of $$n$$ , the graph of $$y = \sqrt[n]{x}$$ is similar to that of $$y = \sqrt{x}$$ . For $$n = 3$$ we have the cube root function $$f(x) = \sqrt[3]{x}$$ whose domain is $$\mathbb{R}$$ (recall that every real number has a cube root) and whose graph is shown in Figure 13(b). The graph of $$y = \sqrt[n]{x}$$ for $$n$$ odd $$\left( {n > 3} \right)$$ is similar to that of $$y = \sqrt[3]{x}$$ .

It enters from the bottom of the third quadrant very close to and to the right of x = negative 2, goes up and to the right through the approximate point (negative 1.6, negative 8), concave down, flattens near the origin, enters into the fourth quadrant, goes steeply down to the right, approaching x = 2, exiting very close to and to the left of x = 2 at the bottom. The third part lies entirely in the third quadrant, mirroring the first part. It enters to the right of the line x = 2 at the top, goes down and to the right, concave up, reaches its low point at approximately (2.7, 30), then goes gently upward to the right, and exits the viewing window at approximately (4.5, 50).

section.paragraph: A function $$f$$ is called an algebraic function if it can be constructed using algebraic operations (such as addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, and taking roots) starting with polynomials. Functions that are not algebraic are called transcendental; these include the trigonometric, exponential, and logarithmic functions.
section.heading: Trigonometric Functions
section.paragraph: Trigonometry and the trigonometric functions are reviewed on The Area Problem and also in Appendix D. In calculus the convention is that radian measure is always used (except when otherwise indicated). For example, when we use the function $$f(x) = \sin x$$ , it is understood that $$\sin x$$ means the sine of the angle whose radian measure is $$x$$ . Thus the graphs of the sine and cosine functions are as shown in Figure 19.

image.alt: Details Two graphs are displayed. In graph a, a sine curve is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The x axis is displayed from negative 3 pi/2 to 3 pi in increments of pi/2. The y axis ranges from negative 1 to 1 in increments of 1 unit. The sine function resembles a wave such that it rises and falls with alternating high and low points at regular intervals, reaching the same y-coordinate for each high point and low point. The sine curve enters the second quadrant above the x axis, rises to the right, reaches a high point at (negative 3 pi/2, 1), goes down and to the right, crosses the x axis at (negative pi, 0), then goes down below the x axis, reaches a low point at (negative pi/2, negative 1), and goes up and to the right through the origin. It then enters into the first quadrant, reaches a high point at (pi/2, 1), goes down and to the right, crosses the x axis at (pi, 0), goes down below the x axis, reaches a low point at (3 pi/2, negative 1), then goes up and to the right through (2 pi, 0), reaches a high point at (5 pi/2, 1). The same pattern then repeats as the curve proceeds to the right. In graph b, a cosine curve is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The x axis ranges from negative 3 pi/2 to 7 pi/2 in increments of pi/2. The y axis ranges from negative 1 to 1 in increments of 1 unit. The cosine curve resembles a wave such that it rises and falls with alternating high and low points at regular intervals, reaching the same y-coordinate for each high point and low point. The cosine curve enters the second quadrant near the x axis, goes down and to the right by crossing the x axis at (negative 3 pi/2, 0), reaches a low point in the third quadrant at (negative pi, negative 1), goes up and to the right through (negative pi/2, 0) and reaches a high point at (0, 1). It then goes down and to the right through (pi/2, 0), reaches a low point at (pi, negative 1), again goes up and to the right through (3 pi/2, 0) to a high point at (2 pi, 1), and goes down and to the right by crossing the x axis at (5 pi/2, 0). The same pattern then repeats as the curve proceeds to the right.

section.paragraph: Notice that for both the sine and cosine functions the domain is $$\left( {- \infty,\infty} \right)$$ and the range is the closed interval $$\left\lbrack {- 1,1} \right\rbrack$$ . Thus, for all values of $$x$$ , we have
$${- 1 \leqslant \sin x \leqslant 1} {- 1 \leqslant \cos x \leqslant 1}$$
or, in terms of absolute values,
$$\left. \left| {\sin x} \right| \leqslant 1 \middle| {\cos x} \middle| \leqslant 1 \right.$$
An important property of the sine and cosine functions is that they are periodic functions and have period $$2\pi$$ . This means that, for all values of $$x$$ ,
$$\sin(x + 2\pi) = \sin x \cos(x + 2\pi) = \cos x$$

The periodic nature of these functions makes them suitable for modeling repetitive phenomena such as tides, vibrating springs, and sound waves. For instance, in Example 1.3.4 we will see that a reasonable model for the number of hours of daylight in Philadelphia $$t$$ days after January 1 is given by the function
$$L(t) = 12 + 2.8\sin{\left\lbrack {\frac{2\pi}{365}\left( {t - 80} \right)} \right\rbrack}$$

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Find the domain of the function $$f(x) = \frac{1}{1 - 2\cos x}$$
Solution This function is defined for all values of $$x$$ except for those that make the denominator $$0$$ . But
$$\left. 1 - 2\cos x = 0 \Leftrightarrow \cos x = \frac{1}{2} \Leftrightarrow x = \frac{\pi}{3} + 2n\pi \right.$$
or
where $$n$$ is any integer (because the cosine function has period $$2\pi$$ ). So the domain of $$f$$ is the set of all real numbers except for the ones noted above.

section.paragraph: The tangent function is related to the sine and cosine functions by the equation
$$\tan x = \frac{\sin x}{\cos x}$$

and its graph is shown in Figure 20. It is undefined whenever $$\cos x = 0$$ , that is, when $${x = \pm \pi \slash 2},{\pm 3\pi \slash 2,\ldots}$$ . Its range is $$\left( {- \infty,\infty} \right)$$ . Notice that the tangent function has period $$\pi$$ :
$$\tan\left( {x + \pi} \right) = \tan x {for all}x$$

image.alt: Details Four dashed vertical lines and a tangent function are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The x axis is displayed from negative 3 pi/2 to 3 pi/2 in increments of pi/2. The y axis is displayed from below 0 to beyond 1 in increments of 1 unit. Dashed vertical lines are drawn parallel to the y axis at the tick marks negative 3 pi/2, negative pi/2, pi/2, and 3 pi/2. The function is a curve with multiple identical parts that are placed one after another, and each part lies between a pair of consecutive dashed vertical lines. The first part of the curve enters from the bottom of the third quadrant to the right of the dashed vertical line at negative 3 pi/2, initially lying close to the dashed line, then increasingly veering off it as the curve rises to the right, crosses the x axis at (negative pi, 0), continues rising upward to the right, veering toward the dashed vertical line at negative pi/2, and eventually exiting very near and to the left of x = negative pi/2. The second part follows the same movement, entering the third quadrant to the right and near the dashed vertical line at negative pi/2, passing through the origin, and exiting to the left and near the dashed vertical line at pi/2. The third part also follows the same movement, entering the fourth quadrant to the right and near the dashed vertical line at pi/2, crossing the x axis at (pi, 0), and exiting to the left and near the dashed vertical line at 3 pi/2. The same pattern repeats as the curve proceeds to the right.

section.paragraph: The remaining three trigonometric functions (cosecant, secant, and cotangent) are the reciprocals of the sine, cosine, and tangent functions. Their graphs are shown in Appendix D.
section.heading: Exponential Functions
section.paragraph: The exponential functions are the functions of the form $$f(x) = b^{ x}$$ , where the base $$b$$ is a positive constant. The graphs of $$y = 2^{ x}$$ and $$y = (0.5)^{x}$$ are shown in Figure 21. In both cases the domain is $$\left( {- \infty,\infty} \right)$$ and the range is $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ .

image.alt: Details Two graphs display two curves on the x y coordinate plane. In the first graph, the curve enters the second quadrant, initially almost coinciding with the negative x axis, begins to veer away from it, goes up and to the right, concave up, crosses the y axis at (0, 1), and continuing to go upward to the right into the first quadrant, exiting the viewing window at the top right. In the second graph, the curve enters the second quadrant at the top left of the viewing window at approximately (negative 2.5, 5.6), goes down and to the right, concave up, crosses the y axis at (0, 1), enters into the first quadrant, and continues to extend toward the x axis, almost coincides with the x axis before exiting near the right extreme of the axis.

section.paragraph: Exponential functions will be studied in detail in Section 1.4, and we will see that they are useful for modeling many natural phenomena, such as when populations grow (if $$b > 1$$ ) or decline (if $$b < 1$$ ).
section.heading: Logarithmic Functions
section.paragraph: The logarithmic functions $$f(x) = \log_{b}x$$ , where the base $$b$$ is a positive constant, are the inverse functions of the exponential functions. They will be studied in Section 1.5. Figure 22 shows the graphs of four logarithmic functions with various bases. In each case the domain is $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ , the range is $$\left( {- \infty,\infty} \right)$$ , and the function increases slowly when $$x > 1$$ .

image.alt: Details Four logarithmic functions with different bases are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. Both the axes are displayed from below 0 to beyond 1 in increments of 1 unit. All four curves enter the fourth quadrant, go up and to the right, concave down, intersect at (1, 0), and exit the first quadrant, thus following a similar shape. The first curve labeled y = log_2(x), enters the fourth quadrant at the bottom near the y axis, goes up and to the right, concave down, crosses the x axis at (1, 0), and exits the first quadrant at the top right. The second curve labeled y = log_3(x) enters the fourth quadrant near the y axis, to the left of the first curve, crosses the x axis at (1, 0), and exits the viewing window below the first curve. The third curve labeled y = log_5(x) enters the fourth quadrant to the left of the second curve, crosses the x axis at (1, 0), and exits the first quadrant below the second curve, a little away from the x axis. The fourth curve labeled y = log_10(x), enters the fourth quadrant very close to the y axis, to the left of the third curve, crosses the x axis at (1, 0), and exits the first quadrant below the third curve, close to the x axis. As the base of the functions increases, the curves become much closer to the axes.

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Classify the following functions as one of the types of functions that we have discussed.
Solution

list.item: (a) $$f{(x)} = 5^{x}$$ is an exponential function. (The variable $$x$$ is the exponent.)
(b) $$g{(x)} = x^{5}$$ is a power function. (The variable $$x$$ is the base.) We could also consider it to be a polynomial of degree $$5$$ .
(c) $$h{(x)} = \frac{1 + x}{1 - \sqrt{x}}$$ is an algebraic function. (It is not a rational function because the denominator is not a polynomial).
(d) $$u{(t)} = 1 - t + 5t^{4}$$ is a polynomial of degree $$4$$ .
